page1_img_1.png.title: Comparison of networks with strong (high modularity) and weak (low modularity) community structure
page1_img_1.png.description: Two side-by-side schematic networks with identical node and edge counts illustrate the difference between strong and weak community structure. The left panel shows three clearly separated communities (dashed outlines) with many dense intra-community edges and only a few inter-community links, corresponding to a high modularity of 0.51. The right panel uses the same nodes and edges but shows many cross-community connections so intra- and inter-community densities are similar, yielding a low modularity of 0.176. The pair demonstrates how modularity captures the quality of a partition: identical-size graphs can have very different community strength depending on link placement.

page5_img_1.png.title: Modularity of DSNs and comparison to Facebook/Cyworld
page5_img_1.png.description: Boxplots of modularity (y-axis) for developer social networks (DSNs) extracted over increasing time windows — 1-month, 3-month, 6-month, 1-year, 2-year and 4-year — plus two general social networks (Facebook and Cyworld) on the x-axis. Each DSN was partitioned repeatedly with the Louvain algorithm (50 perturbed runs), so the boxes show the distribution of modularity scores: the 1-month DSN has the highest median (~0.57) and thereafter median modularity generally declines (6-month and longer DSNs medians ≈0.38–0.48) though all DSNs remain above the 0.3 threshold. Facebook and Cyworld exhibit even higher median modularity (~0.62 and ~0.60 respectively). Small circles mark outliers, indicating some variability across runs but a clear pattern that DSNs possess significant community structure which tends to be stronger in shorter time slices and is comparable, though somewhat lower on average, than these GSNs.

page6_img_1.png.title: Evolution of active developers (old vs new) 2000–2009
page6_img_1.png.description: Stacked half-year bars show the number of active developers in Mozilla from 2000fh to 2009sh, with black segments for developers who were active in earlier periods (old) and gray for newcomers (new). The total developer count rises to a peak around 2001–2003 (roughly 1,000–1,200 developers), then exhibits a sharp drop around 2004 (the paper notes a drop from about 1,093 to 533), after which totals stabilize in the ~500–1,000 range. Early periods (2000–2004) feature a large fraction of new developers (over ~39% per the text), while after 2004 the influx of newcomers is smaller and the old/deeply active cohort constitutes a larger share of each period’s bar.

page4_img_fig4.png.title: CCDF of developer degree for multiple DSN time windows vs power-law references
page4_img_fig4.png.description: Log–log complementary cumulative degree distributions (P(degree ≥ x)) for six Mozilla DSNs extracted over different time windows (blue: 1-month, red: 3-month, green: 6-month, purple: 1-year, pink: 2-year, gray: 4-year) are plotted with reference straight lines showing typical power‑law slopes from other social systems (γ = −2.412 for Twitter, −2.38 for the blogosphere, and two Cyworld slopes −2 and −5). The DSN curves fall away from those straight reference lines (they bend/curve rather than follow a single linear slope), and longer aggregation periods (e.g., 4-year) extend the tail to larger maximum degrees but still do not produce a clear power‑law straight line. As reported in the paper, quantitative tests (Clauset et al. method) yielded p-values < 0.1 for these DSNs, supporting the visual conclusion that none of the DSN degree distributions follow a power law even though they do show many low-degree nodes and a small fraction of higher-degree hubs.

page5_img_2.png.title: Community size distributions for DSNs (absolute and normalized)
page5_img_2.png.description: Two panels of boxplots compare community sizes across developer social networks (DSNs) extracted over increasing time windows. The left panel shows absolute community sizes for 1‑month, 3‑month, 6‑month, 1‑year, 2‑year and 4‑year DSNs: medians remain small (about 23–55 members) while the spread and extreme values grow with longer windows (the largest communities are reported as 83 members for 1‑month and 718 for 4‑year). The right panel shows normalized community size (proportion of the whole network) and includes Amazon for reference: the biggest DSN communities account for roughly 21%–36% of users and the ten largest communities encompass almost all users, and the normalized distributions are similar to Amazon’s despite large absolute size differences.

page6_img_2.png.title: Evolution of cumulative degree distributions in Mozilla DSNs (2000–2009)
page6_img_2.png.description: Log-scale complementary cumulative degree distributions (CCDF) for half‑year Mozilla developer social networks (legend lists periods from 2000fh to 2009sh) are plotted: the x‑axis is node degree and the y‑axis is the CCDF on a logarithmic scale. Each colored curve shows the fraction of developers with degree ≥ d for a specific half‑year; early periods (dark blues, 2000–2002) exhibit heavier tails (extend farther right) indicating a larger fraction of high‑degree developers, while later periods (reds through light blues, post‑2003) show steeper drops and the curves cluster more tightly. The curved, non‑linear shapes across the range (rather than a single straight line on the log plot) visually support the paper’s finding that DSN degree distributions do not follow a strict power law and that the distribution stabilized into a narrower form after the mid‑2000s.

page2_img_figure_1.png.title: Example: building a weighted developer network from bug comments
page2_img_figure_1.png.description: The figure has three panels showing the transformation from bug reports to a pruned developer social network. (a) Four bug reports contain symbols that map to four developers (David: star, Bob: triangle, Jack: circle, Bill: square), indicating which developers commented on each bug. (b) Those co‑comment relationships are converted into a weighted undirected graph (ovals are developers; edge labels are counts of shared bug comments, e.g., Bob–Jack = 4, David–Bill = 1, several pairwise edges = 2). (c) After removing edges with weight ≤ 3 (the paper’s threshold to drop casual ties), only the strong Bob–Jack connection remains, illustrating how pruning yields a smaller core developer graph.

page2_img_table_1.png.title: Subject periods with developer and bug-report counts for DSNs
page2_img_table_1.png.description: Table I lists the six time-window subjects used to extract developer social networks (columns: Dec. 2009 (1 month), Oct.–Dec. 2009 (3 months), Jul.–Dec. 2009 (6 months), Jan.–Dec. 2009 (1 year), Jan. 2008–Dec. 2009 (2 years), and Jan. 2006–Dec. 2009 (4 years)). For each period it reports the number of developers remaining after filtering versus the total observed (e.g., 387 remained of 2,996 total for the 1‑month window; 2,865 remained of 51,692 total for the 4‑year window) and the number of bug reports used (ranging from 10,586 for 1 month up to 246,331 for 4 years). The “remained/total” distinction reflects the paper’s removal of low-weight edges and casual users so the table highlights that the raw contributor pool grows with longer windows while the core, active developer set used in the DSNs is much smaller.

page4_img_fig5.png.title: Degree-of-separation distributions for Mozilla DSNs and sampled GSNs
page4_img_fig5.png.description: This line plot shows the probability distribution of shortest-path distances (x-axis: distance between two developers, y-axis: probability) for six Mozilla DSNs (1-month, 3-month, 6-month, 1-year, 2-year, 4-year) and two sampled general social networks (Twitter, 8000 sample; Cyworld, 3000 sample). The DSN curves are tightly concentrated with a clear peak at distance ≈3 (with some mass at 4), meaning most developer pairs are three hops apart (the paper reports average path lengths ≈2.9–3.4 and >90% of pairs within a few hops). By contrast, the Twitter and Cyworld samples peak farther right (around distance 4) and exhibit a broader tail to larger distances, supporting the paper’s claim that developer social networks constitute a “smaller world” than these general social networks.

page3_img_1.png.title: Detected communities mapped to BOF meetings with overlap percentages
page3_img_1.png.description: Top row shows identified communities as circles (radius ∝ number of developers) and the bottom row lists BOF (birds‑of‑a‑feather) meetings. Directed arrows connect each detected community to BOF meetings and are annotated with overlap fractions (for example 0.70 and 1.0) that indicate the proportion of a BOF’s participants contained in that community. The rightmost community (labeled A) contains 70% of BOF X and 100% of BOF Y, illustrating that a single detected community can encompass multiple BOF meetings. The visualization demonstrates that Louvain‑detected communities largely correspond to offline BOF groups (most BOFs map predominantly into one community, with few splits).

page7_img_1.png.title: Evolution of degree-of-separation in Mozilla developer networks (2000–2009)
page7_img_1.png.description: Overlaid probability distributions of shortest-path distances between developer pairs for half‑year periods from 2000 to 2009. Each curve (legend shows period and its average path length, APL) peaks at distance 2–3 with peak probability around 0.45–0.55, indicating most developer pairs are two or three hops apart; the APL slowly increases from about 2.45 (2000fh) to about 3.02 (2009sh). The tail beyond distance 6 is negligible, so the vast majority of pairs remain reachable within a few hops across all periods. This small rightward shift over time corresponds to the paper’s observation that average path length grew slightly but the DSN retained a “small world” (most pairs within 3–4 hops) throughout the decade.

page8_img_1.png.title: Taxonomy of community evolution patterns
page8_img_1.png.description: A two-column table enumerating six community-evolution patterns (Expand, Shrink, Merge, Split, Extinct, Emerge) with concise definitions for each. "Expand" and "Shrink" describe size changes when a community’s prior set is a single community (respectively indicating newcomer influx or member loss); "Merge" and "Split" denote communities combining or dividing across periods and imply shared interests or interest divergence. "Extinct" means a community has no successor (members left or dispersed) and "Emerge" means a community has no predecessor (a new interest area appears). The paper uses this refined taxonomy (with community similarity threshold ε=0.3 to link communities across consecutive periods) to classify and interpret community paths in the Mozilla developer social network.

page7_img_2.png.title: Evolution of Modularity in Mozilla DSN (2000–2009)
page7_img_2.png.description: Boxplots of modularity values (y-axis) for successive half‑year periods from 2000fh to 2009sh (x-axis) are plotted, with a red line tracing the central trend across runs. Each box summarizes the distribution of modularity obtained from repeated Louvain runs (multiple experiments with 50 perturbed node orderings), so the spread shows algorithmic variability and sensitivity to input ordering. The plot shows a clear upward trend: median modularity rises from about 0.18–0.20 in the 2000 periods to roughly 0.50–0.52 by 2009fh, with the medians crossing the 0.3 threshold after mid‑2003—indicating that communities in the Mozilla developer social network became increasingly well defined and stable over the decade, despite some period-to-period fluctuations.

page7_img_3.png.title: Evolution of community size distribution (2000–2009)
page7_img_3.png.description: Boxplots of community sizes for consecutive half-year periods from 2000fh to 2009sh, with the y-axis showing community size and each boxplot showing median, IQR, whiskers and outliers. The early years (roughly 2000–2003) display much larger variance and several large outliers (points reaching above 300 members, e.g., around 2002sh), whereas after ~2004 the boxes narrow and medians drop so that most communities have sizes well below ~75. The overlaid trend line (red) and median bars show no sustained upward or downward trend — sizes fluctuate but stabilize in the latter half of the decade, supporting the paper’s claim that community sizes remain generally small with greater instability early in the project.

page9_img_1.png.title: Mozilla developer community evolution (2000–2009)
page9_img_1.png.description: A time-ordered evolution diagram (half-year periods p2000f through p2009s down the left) where each circle is a detected developer community and its radius is proportional to the number of developers in that community. Directed edges connect communities across consecutive periods to show evolution (derivation, merges, splits, emergence, extinction), and several paths are highlighted: a bold outlined path tracking Firefox-related communities that emerge around 2004 and grow substantially by 2008–2009, a long-lived Bugzilla path spanning 2001–2009 that shows a shrink after the Firefox 1.5 period, and other paths (e.g., security and Rhino) that exhibit split/merge behavior. The figure visually supports the paper’s findings that before 2005 many communities were isolated and volatile, while after the 2004 releases communities become more stable and display the labeled evolution patterns (emerge, expand, shrink, split, merge, extinct) linked to project events.
